content:
Yellow alert automatically issued when extreme heat warning takes effect

The new mechanism announced today by the Labour Department continues to adopt the Observatory's Heat Index, but adds two new conditions on top of the existing warning trigger thresholds, lowering the bar for issuing alerts. The first condition is that when the Observatory issues an Extreme Heat Weather Special Alert, the department will automatically issue a yellow heat stress warning, while at the same time lowering the thresholds for red and black warnings: previously, issuing a red warning required a Heat Index reading of 32 or above recorded at the King's Park monitoring station, or at four out of the other nine monitoring stations; under the new mechanism, if the Observatory has already issued an Extreme Heat Weather Special Alert, a reading of 32 at the King's Park monitoring station, or at just two out of the other nine stations, will suffice. According to Observatory data, the "Extreme Heat Weather" special alert refers to situations where temperatures have already reached, or are expected to generally reach, an extreme level of 35.0 degrees or above, reminding the public that weather conditions are extremely hot and urging them to pay attention to their physical health.

If multiple areas reach 35 degrees with sufficient data, yellow alert will be directly "upgraded" to red

Another new condition under the new mechanism is that when temperatures across multiple areas of Hong Kong reach 35 degrees or above, in addition to the further lowering of the index thresholds for triggering warnings mentioned above, existing heat stress warnings will also be automatically raised by one level. Hui Chak-sum gave an example: if multiple areas reach above 35 degrees and there is sufficient data to trigger a yellow heat stress warning, a red warning will be issued directly as an "upgrade"; and when the threshold for a red warning is met, a black warning will be issued directly.

The new mechanism takes effect tomorrow (the 28th). Hui Chak-sum said that although this year's summer is nearly over, hot weather may continue, and it is impossible to estimate whether temperatures will rise abnormally again, in which case the new mechanism can be applied. Two former Observatory directors had earlier written articles pointing out that the authorities had misapplied the Observatory's Heat Index, arguing that it fails to reflect the conditions faced by outdoor workers, and suggested adopting the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature used in many countries. The Labour Department said that after the mechanism is launched, it will continuously review its operation and make ongoing improvements, such as researching whether to add Wet Bulb Globe Temperature and other monitoring data as system indicators.

Under the new mechanism, the hottest day of 8.9 would have triggered a red warning

After the Labour Department's secretary met with the press, he further briefed the media. The department cited the example that on 9 August, when temperatures broke records, a red heat stress warning would have been issued under the new mechanism. On 8 August, temperatures were relatively lower, but wind speed and humidity were unfavourable, and a black warning might have been issued. Under the new mechanism, there may be four to seven days per year when a red warning would be issued, and one to two days when a black warning might be issued.

Lam Chiu-ying: Continuing to use Hong Kong Heat Index is a "defect that needs to be addressed"

Former Observatory director Lam Chiu-ying, who has repeatedly criticised the existing work heat stress warning mechanism, described the new arrangement as "a step forward," believing that incorporating temperature into consideration is a down-to-earth and easily understood indicator for workers, and meets the expectations of frontline workers. However, he described the continued use of the Hong Kong Heat Index in the warning mechanism as "a defect that needs to be addressed," saying, "There is no reason for us to use an unscientific (mechanism) as the basis and then use other methods to correct it." He expects the authorities to formally adopt the internationally used Wet Bulb Globe Temperature before next summer. Lam Chiu-ying also pointed out that the warning thresholds are only the starting point; measures to cool down workers are merely guidelines, and workers have reported that they are seldom effectively implemented. He suggested that such measures be made statutory requirements.

Lee Boon-ying: New mechanism is a "minor patch"

Another former director, Lee Boon-ying, also reiterated that the research on the Hong Kong Heat Index is not applicable to outdoor workers, and that the Labour Department's application of the Hong Kong Heat Index is "scientifically untenable." He described the main addition of considering temperature in the new mechanism as a "minor patch" that fails to fully account for factors such as humidity and wind, "only addressing the predicament of having no higher-level work heat stress warning when extreme high temperatures occur," emphasising that the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature has proven effective in many countries. He said that Hong Kong's hot weather season is not yet over, protection for outdoor workers remains inadequate, and they can only look out for themselves.

ICRC suggests subsidising Wet Bulb Globe Index equipment at worksites

The Industrial Injuries Compensation Rights Association said it was pleased to see the authorities improve the mechanism, pointing out that the Observatory's Extreme Heat Weather Special Alert has a warning nature, and incorporating the special alert into consideration would, it believes, make it easier to trigger higher-level warnings, reflecting the heat stress faced by outdoor workers. The association also recommended that the government promote and subsidise companies in installing Wet Bulb Globe Index monitoring equipment at worksites, so that employers can adjust work arrangements according to on-site conditions.

The association also pointed out that if workers' working conditions do not improve after warnings are issued, the warnings would be useless. It suggested improving the existing "Guidelines on Prevention of Heat Stroke at Work" to stipulate that when a black heat stress warning is issued, high-risk outdoor work must be suspended; for other levels, workers should be guaranteed the right to take rest as needed, and employers must not impose penalties.

Greenpeace said this adjustment is old wine in a new bottle. Without using the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature and continuing to use the "Hong Kong Heat Index" that does not meet actual needs, it cannot reflect the actual heat stress faced by outdoor workers, and protection is limited. Greenpeace project officer Yeung Kit-lai said this update is like scratching the surface through a boot. She pointed out that the conditions for issuing red and black work heat stress warnings still rely on the Hong Kong Heat Index, which has a relatively low weighting for "heat radiation" and is unsuitable for measuring the heat stress of outdoor workers, lacking a scientific basis. She said that the Labour Department's continued use of an incorrect indicator greatly reduces protection for workers.
